source_user: Advanced cluster case RoCE-47: Diagnose a RoCE-based GPU cluster whose collective communication has unstable tail latency. Variant 47 must state assumptions, define a falsifiable hypothesis, name metrics, and include one failure or rollback condition.
source_assistant: An expert answer should distinguish model-domain mechanisms from runtime measurements. Required technical anchors: check lossless-priority configuration, PFC/ECN, MTU, route symmetry, congestion, NIC counters, queue pairs, and whether a fallback path is hiding the real fault. It must report topology, workload, units, baselines, confounders, and evidence needed before claiming improvement.
corrected_answer:
Assume a multi-node GPU collective over a RoCE fabric, and verify NIC and switch models, VLAN/priority mapping, MTU, routes, congestion-control settings, collective-library version, GPU/NIC placement, and software versions before changing anything. The data path is a testable model: the library posts verbs work requests to queue pairs using registered buffers; Ethernet carries the traffic along the selected routes; completions, retransmissions, PFC/ECN reactions, timeouts, and any fallback transport determine the application-visible result. RoCE is not inherently lossless or low-tail, so a low device-counter rate or an apparently successful collective does not prove that the intended path is healthy.

Hypothesis: with model, message-size distribution, node count, topology, routes, MTU, traffic mix, software, clocks, and background load held constant, correcting the suspected priority/congestion/MTU/routing condition reduces collective p95 and p99 latency (ms) and timeout/retry rate while preserving achieved bandwidth (GB/s) and application throughput (samples/s or tokens/s). First establish a known-good baseline and repeat matched A/B runs. Record per-operation timestamps, p50/p95/p99/max latency, payload bytes, achieved bandwidth, collective time fraction, queue-pair completions and errors, retransmissions, ECN marks, PFC pause frames and duration, NIC drops, link utilization, switch queue occupancy, GPU/NIC PCIe placement, and CPU/GPU utilization. Correlate device counters with application traces; distinguish congestion from synchronization, incast, oversubscription, route asymmetry, host scheduling, thermal effects, and a fallback path.

Triage non-destructively: compare both endpoints and all hops, verify the intended priority consistently maps to PFC and ECN, check MTU end to end, inspect route symmetry and ECMP distribution, and compare counters before and after a controlled single-variable change. Use a canary subset and bounded-duration load; do not disable PFC, alter congestion thresholds, or drain production traffic globally without an approved change and rollback. Roll back immediately if p99 or timeout/error rates worsen, pauses spread, drops appear, throughput falls beyond the predeclared tolerance, or collective correctness is affected; preserve traces and revert the last change. Evidence is required before claiming a fix: configuration snapshots, topology and route dumps, synchronized application/device traces, repeated confidence intervals or distributions, and a fault-injection or canary result showing the same signature and recovery.
risks: platform-specific RoCE behavior and counter names may differ
fallback traffic can mask the primary path fault
tail latency is confounded by topology, synchronization, and workload mix
unsafe fabric changes can amplify congestion or disrupt collectives
evidence_required: verified end-to-end topology, MTU, priority/PFC/ECN, route, and software configuration
matched repeated baseline and single-variable A/B traces
application and NIC/switch counters with timestamps and units
canary or controlled fault-injection result plus tested rollback evidence

Triage non-destructively: compare both endpoints and all hops, verify the intended priority consistently maps to PFC and ECN, check MTU end to end, inspect route symmetry and ECMP distribution, and compare counters before and after a controlled single-variable change. Use a canary subset and bounded-duration load; do not disable PFC, alter congestion thresholds, or drain production traffic globally without an approved change and rollback. Roll back immediately if p99 or timeout/error rates worsen, pauses spread, drops appear, throughput falls beyond the predeclared tolerance, or collective correctness is affected; preserve traces and revert the last change. Evidence is required before claiming a fix: configuration snapshots, topology and route dumps, synchronized application/device traces, repeated confidence intervals or distributions, and a fault-injection or canary result showing the same signature and recovery.
risks: platform-specific RoCE behavior and counter names may differ
fallback traffic can mask the primary path fault
tail latency is confounded by topology, synchronization, and workload mix
unsafe fabric changes can amplify congestion or disrupt collectives
evidence_required: verified end-to-end topology, MTU, priority/PFC/ECN, route, and software configuration
matched repeated baseline and single-variable A/B traces
application and NIC/switch counters with timestamps and units
canary or controlled fault-injection result plus tested rollback evidence
